rows.notes: The study is explicitly a literature review (labelled 'Review'; objectives are to review the state of irrigated agriculture in the HPA and discuss three management/technology approaches). Its only own analysis is a descriptive processing of satellite-derived soil moisture (SMOS/Palmer) and GRACE groundwater storage percentiles for the three HPA regions, 2010-2019 (Section 3.2, Figure 7), which concerns drought and groundwater storage, not sub-surface drip irrigation. All statements on SDI (water use reduction up to 45%, application efficiency up to 97%, Nebraska and Texas corn results, cotton/sorghum results) are drawn from cited work [67-73]. The claim that SDI could extend aquifer lifespan in vulnerable regions is a discussion/recommendation (Section 4.3, Conclusions), not an own result.

Review article; no own experiment, survey or model on soil moisture sensors. The statements that sensor-based scheduling reduced irrigation water use in Kansas groundwater management districts, that Texas could save about $10 million, and that Nebraska growers with sensors save water are all cited from other sources [61,62,64]; the figure that 11.5% of HPA farms use sensors comes from the USDA Irrigation and Water Management Survey [9]. The own satellite soil moisture/GRACE analysis (Section 3.2) does not involve sensors or scheduling. The claim that sensor-based scheduling could extend aquifer life is the authors' discussion (Section 4.2), not an own finding.

notes: Full text appears complete (Sections 1-5 plus references). The paper is a literature review with a small secondary analysis of public remote-sensing datasets (soil moisture and groundwater storage percentiles by HPA region); that analysis does not bear on either cited technology, so both rows are rated as non-primary with no own evidence on the claims.
